CausalChain: Fibrotic liver disease -> Increased ECM stiffness -> Activation of integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK (and YAP/TAZ) signaling in resident macrophages -> Polarization into M2-like, immunosuppressive TAMs -> Secretion of TGF-β, LOXL2 and ECM remodeling enzymes -> Further increase in matrix stiffness -> Reinforcement of tumor-promoting microenvironment
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in the fibrotic liver, increased ECM stiffness initiates a self-reinforcing mechanotransduction loop by activating integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in resident macrophages, which drives their polarization toward a tumor-supportive M2 phenotype. These M2-like TAMs secrete factors—including TGF-β, LOXL2, and other ECM remodeling enzymes—that further enhance matrix stiffness and perpetuate a tumor-promoting microenvironment conducive to HCC progression. Additionally, we postulate that compensatory mechanosensitive pathways such as YAP/TAZ may be engaged under conditions of high stiffness, further sustaining the M2 state. Consequently, the simultaneous application of integrin/FAK inhibitors (and potentially YAP/TAZ modulators), guided by real-time monitoring with single-cell transcriptomic profiling and stiffness-sensing technologies, will disrupt this feed-forward loop by repolarizing TAMs to an M1 phenotype, thereby impeding liver cancer progression.
Abstract: This study proposes a refined mechanistic model in which fibrotic liver disease promotes a self-reinforcing loop that drives hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression. In our model, increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness in fibrotic livers activates integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in resident macrophages, thereby driving their polarization toward an immunosuppressive, tumor-promoting M2 phenotype. These M2-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) secrete key ECM remodeling factors such as TGF-β and LOXL2, which further stiffen the matrix and fortify a pro-tumor microenvironment. To augment the practical implementability of this hypothesis, we integrate cutting-edge techniques including single-cell transcriptomics, real-time stiffness sensors, and advanced imaging to concurrently monitor mechanotransduction and cellular phenotypes. Moreover, we propose that additional mechanosensitive pathways (e.g., YAP/TAZ) may compensate for or amplify integrin/FAK signaling under high-stiffness conditions. Targeting these signaling cascades using selective inhibitors could interrupt the feedback loop, repolarize TAMs toward an M1 phenotype, and ultimately suppress HCC progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain—starting with fibrotic liver disease leading to increased ECM stiffness, which activates integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in macrophages, resulting in M2 polarization, the secretion of matrix stiffening factors, and the maintenance of a tumorigenic microenvironment. However, it now incorporates modern technological strategies (single-cell transcriptomics, real-time stiffness sensors, and advanced imaging) to enhance empirical testing and mechanistic clarity. Additionally, the refined hypothesis acknowledges the potential contribution of parallel mechanotransduction pathways, such as YAP/TAZ, addressing concerns regarding compensatory mechanisms. This detailed approach improves the practical applicability of targeting the self-reinforcing loop to reprogram TAMs and suppress HCC progression.
